Upper-body garments (T-shirt, pullover, dress, coat, shirt) are a body outline with neck, shoulder, chest, waist and hip widths plus two sleeve polygons, whose length depends on the class (vest, cap, short, mid, three-quarter, long, jacket length). Trousers are a waistband and two legs with a crotch fork. Sneakers and ankle boots are single side-view outlines with toe, tongue or shaft, heel and sole. Sandals are a sole, an optional heel block and several thin straps. Bags are a body with an optional arched handle. Each drawing gets a small random horizontal shear, is filled on a 48 by 48 grid, averaged down to 24 by 24, and stretched to fill its own bounding box. Footwear and bags are drawn upright. Each drawing is stored only as its quantised shape descriptor: a 12 by 12 coarse occupancy grid, four 12-band outline depth profiles and log aspect ratio, 193 values.

stages.name: Foreground and bounding box
stages.computes: Grey levels are turned into a soft 'item present' map relative to the image's brightest pixel. A row or column counts as part of the item if its total occupancy beats a small threshold scaled to the busiest row or column. That gives a tight bounding box and the item's width-to-height ratio.

key_numbers.meaning: grey level below which a pixel counts as background (fraction of the image's brightest grey level)
grey-level ramp above that floor before a pixel counts as fully part of the item
minimum summed occupancy for a row or column to be inside the box: 4.9% of the busiest line, clamped to between 0.46 and 1.05 pixel units

stages.name: Normalise to box
stages.computes: The box contents are resampled with smooth interpolation to fill a fixed square, which removes position and size and also stretches the item so its aspect ratio is lost. The ratio is kept as a separate number. The occupancy map goes to a coarse square for shape tests and the raw grey levels go to a finer square for texture tests.

key_numbers.meaning: resolution of the stretched occupancy silhouette
resolution of the stretched grey-level image used for interior detail

stages.name: Shape descriptor
stages.computes: The silhouette is summarised as a 12 by 12 grid of coverage, plus how far one must travel in from the left, right, top and bottom edges before hitting the outline, measured in 12 bands, plus the log of the width-to-height ratio. Each part has a fixed weight and the values are rounded. A left-right mirrored version is also computed.

key_numbers.meaning: coarse coverage grid over the box
occupancy level at which the outline is considered reached when measuring edge depths
weight of the log aspect ratio relative to coverage cells (weight 25) and edge-depth bands (weights 40 to 47)

stages.name: Template matching per class
stages.computes: For each class, the descriptor is compared by squared difference with all 3,200 stored drawings of that class. The 16 closest are kept, and the class distance is mostly their average with some weight on the single closest. For sandals, sneakers and ankle boots, the mirrored silhouette is also tried and the better of the two is kept, so the toe can point either way.

key_numbers.meaning: number of nearest stored drawings averaged per class
weight on the average of the 16 nearest versus the single nearest

stages.name: Garment proportions
stages.computes: Row-by-row widths of the silhouette are measured in from both sides, along with the empty space inside each row's extent. From these come shoulder, cuff, waist and hem widths, sleeve overhang beyond the body, flare, a gap between dangling sleeves or legs, a scooped top edge, the width of the connected central body only (waist and hip), and a curved shirt-tail hem. These are combined into soft cues: tee-like short sleeves, long arms, skirt or dress, tank top, A-line, square body, long coat, loose blouse.

key_numbers.meaning: bands taken as shoulder, waist and hem of the stretched item
width/height ratio below which an item counts as narrow (dress or trouser-like)
how much shoulder or cuff width must exceed waist or hem width (fraction of box width) before sleeves count as sticking out

stages.name: Interior detail (tops)
stages.computes: On the grey-level image, scaled by its 80th-percentile brightness, the method looks for a persistent vertical line or a row of bright points near the centre front, compared against the side panels. It searches three slight tilts and several column offsets and keeps the strongest (zip, placket, buttons). It also measures all-over texture versus a texture patch confined to the chest (logo), vertical versus horizontal contrast (drape, stripes), neckline shape from the top outline (collar peak, scoop, raised collar), V-shaped light or dark wedges below the neck (lining, V-neck, lapels), fine centre seams, and a horizontal waistband line near the hem. The results are added to the T-shirt, pullover, coat and shirt scores with fixed weights.

key_numbers.meaning: centre-front strip searched for a zip or placket, allowing a slight slant
upper chest versus lower torso texture comparison used to detect a chest logo
brightness reference used to normalise the interior contrast

stages.name: Upper-body group decision
stages.computes: T-shirt and long-sleeve scores start from the template distances and are adjusted by the proportion cues. Pullover, coat and shirt share the long-sleeve score and are told apart by the interior detail relative to the best of the three. The shirt takes the best of a tee-like route, a long-sleeve route and a loose blouse route. The T-shirt is penalised when shirt detail clearly beats T-shirt detail. The dress score gets the skirt, A-line and long-body cues.

key_numbers.meaning: margin by which shirt detail must exceed T-shirt detail before the T-shirt is penalised
weight of the template-distance difference when choosing among pullover, coat and shirt

stages.name: Trouser test
stages.computes: Looks for a slit of empty space in the lower centre with cloth on both sides of it (two legs), a full flat top band (waistband), and a top wider than the bottom. These raise the trouser score and lower the dress score.

key_numbers.meaning: region checked for an empty gap between legs
minimum row-wise coverage in that region below which a leg gap counts

stages.name: Footwear tests
stages.computes: Top and bottom outlines are traced per column, and the item is oriented so the taller end is on a fixed side. The method then measures holes inside the outline (straps), background enclosed between strap material, empty space under the arch (heel), the height step from toe to shaft (boot), a rise to a tongue then a drop (sneaker), a flat high plateau (boot), valleys in the top line (open vamp), elongation and total covered area. These push sandal, sneaker and boot scores up or down.

key_numbers.meaning: rows (of 24) by which the shaft end must stand taller than the toe end before the item starts to count as a boot
width/height ratio above which a long, low shoe looks like a sneaker
covered fraction of the box below which an airy item looks like a sandal
rows of dip in the top outline after a local rise before it counts as an open vamp

stages.name: Bag tests
stages.computes: Looks for an empty region in the upper middle (under a handle) above a solid lower panel, with supports on both sides. Also looks for a wide, left-right symmetric box, or a near-perfect rectangle with no internal gap. These raise the bag score.

key_numbers.meaning: region expected to be empty under a handle
coverage of the lower body band above which it counts as a solid bag panel
left-right asymmetry below which a wide item counts as symmetric

d.decision: Each class score starts as the negated template-match distance. The geometric and texture cue terms are added to it. The upper-body classes are partly rebuilt from shared group scores (T-shirt-like versus long-sleeved), with relative detail scores splitting pullover, coat and shirt, and the shirt taking the best of several routes. The class with the highest final score is chosen.
d.adapts_per_image: Several steps depend on the image. The bounding box is found per image, with thresholds scaled to that image's brightest pixel and busiest row or column, and the item is stretched to fill it. Interior contrast is normalised by the image's 80th-percentile brightness. Matching keeps the 16 nearest stored drawings per class, and for footwear the better of normal and mirrored orientation. Footwear outlines are flipped so the taller end is on a fixed side. The zip and placket search keeps the best over three tilts and several column offsets, and the collar search keeps the best over several wedge sizes. Several scores take the best of alternative routes, such as the shirt score and the pullover, coat and shirt split relative to their best.

d.summary: The item is first cut out as a soft silhouette. The silhouette is cropped to its extent, rescaled to fill the frame, and compared with about 22,000 synthetic silhouettes drawn from 43 hand-designed clothing, shoe and bag styles. Each style is scored by how close its nearest few drawings are, and the style scores are pooled into a prior for each of the 10 classes. A long series of hand-built shape and texture cues then adds to or subtracts from these class scores: necklines, a centre zip or placket, sleeve length, leg split, skirt flare, prints, sandal straps, sneaker tongue, boot shaft and bag handle. The class with the highest adjusted score wins.
d.references: About 22,000 binary silhouettes, drawn at 42x42 from parametric polygons with random proportions, a small random shift and a slight slant. There are 43 styles, each with 180 to 1200 drawings. Garments drawn from the front: tee, tank, strappy top, boxy top, sweater, V-neck sweater, jacket, coat, shirt, blouse, short-sleeve blouse, cardigan, short, sleeveless, long and straight dresses, long-sleeve tee, fitted top, tunic, loose tee, muscle top and swing coat. Trousers: narrow, wide, and wide with a high split. Bags: handle bag, tote, strap bag, backpack, clutch, satchel and shoulder bag, with handles and straps drawn as arcs. Shoes in side view: trainer, high sneaker, boot, heeled boot, hiker, sandal, heel, wedge, slide, mule and sport strap sandal. Bags are mirrored at random, and a few shoes are mirrored. Each drawing is kept only as a compact shape summary: a 14x14 coarse coverage grid plus the first-edge depth seen from each of the four sides in 14 strips. A fixed table assigns styles to classes with hand-set mixing weights. The T-shirt class, for example, draws on tee, tank, strappy, long tee, loose tee and muscle top.

stages.name: Brightness normalisation and soft silhouette
stages.computes: Divides the image by a bright reference level: the 705th darkest of the 784 pixels, so roughly the 90th percentile, with a floor. A soft per-pixel coverage map then rises from the background level to full item coverage, blended with a lightly blurred version so that antialiased edges count as partial coverage. A brightness-normalised copy capped at twice the reference is kept for the texture cues.

key_numbers.meaning: the 705th darkest of 784 pixels sets the reference brightness, about the 90th percentile
lowest allowed reference brightness, on the 0 to 1 grey scale
normalised brightness range over which a pixel goes from background to fully covered

stages.name: Crop and rescale
stages.computes: Finds the first and last rows and columns that hold real coverage. It then resamples the silhouette, centred on that box, so its longer side spans the full 28-pixel frame, using bilinear interpolation.

key_numbers.meaning: a row or column counts as occupied only if one pixel reaches this coverage and its total coverage reaches this sum
smallest box size, so tiny items are not blown up too far

stages.name: Shape summary
stages.computes: Averages the rescaled silhouette into a 14x14 grid of 2x2 blocks, blended 55/45 with a smoothed copy. It then measures, scanning from the left, right, top and bottom, how far in the first covered pixel lies on each scanline, capped at half the width, and averages these depths over 14 strips per side. The result has 196 + 56 numbers.

key_numbers.meaning: coarse coverage grid over the framed item
coverage level that counts as hitting the item's edge
cap on edge depth, also used for empty scanlines

stages.name: Nearest-drawing matching per style
stages.computes: Takes the squared distance from the image's shape summary to every stored drawing. For each of the 43 styles it keeps the 8 closest drawings and scores the style as the negative of a blend of their mean distance (70%) and the single closest distance (30%), times 0.58.

key_numbers.meaning: number of nearest drawings kept per style
weight on the mean versus the minimum of those 8 distances
scale turning distance into a log-likelihood-like score

stages.name: Style-to-class prior
stages.computes: Each of the 10 class scores starts as a weighted soft maximum (log of a weighted sum of exponentials) of its member styles' scores, with hand-set weights. A style can feed more than one class: the shirt score, for example, also draws on tee, tank and sweater.

stages.name: Upper-body garment cues
stages.computes: Finds the item's vertical centre line as the median of the row centroids. Along that line it measures: a straight vertical zip or placket against the nearby fabric; paired diagonal lapel edges near the top; whether the neckline rises above the shoulders (a collar) or dips below them (a scoop); chest-only graphics against all-over print; whether the hem dips at the centre (a shirt tail); and air gaps between the sleeves and the body. These cues push pullover, coat, shirt and T-shirt up or down.

key_numbers.meaning: how close to the centre line a vertical seam must lie to count as a zip or placket
vertical band of the frame searched for a placket

key_numbers.value: 4, 7, 11 px deep with spreads 2.7 and 4.6 px
key_numbers.meaning: lapel V shapes tested below the neck
rows checked for gaps between sleeve and body

stages.name: Width profile: trousers versus dress
stages.computes: Measures the item's width at the shoulder rows (4 to 9), waist (11 to 15) and hem (21 to 24). From these it scores skirt flare and a narrow top. It looks for a dark split between two legs in rows 16 to 25, or a dark crease line between bright legs, and for a flat waistband across the top. These cues add to or subtract from the trouser and dress scores, and the leg-split cue also lowers the pullover, coat and dress scores.

key_numbers.meaning: hem width minus waist width over which flare goes from none to full
shoulder width below which a top counts as slim, suggesting a dress
coverage drop between the thighs and the centre needed to count as split legs

stages.name: Sleeve length and knit cues
stages.computes: Compares the lowest covered point near each outer side (the sleeve cuff) with the centre hem. A large rise means short sleeves (a tee); cuffs at or below the hem mean long sleeves. It also checks for a horizontal ribbed band just above the hem (a knit waistband), a neck notch, fabric texture that runs in both directions, stripes that run one way only, a centre front opening, and print on the sleeves.

key_numbers.meaning: cuff height above the hem that marks short sleeves
smaller cuff drop, read as a partly shortened sleeve
where the ribbed waistband is looked for

stages.name: Bag cues
stages.computes: In the band from 32% to 60% of the item's height it looks for a central hole flanked by solid sides, with solid material below: a handle loop. It also looks for a broad, straight-sided body. Both cues raise the bag score.

key_numbers.meaning: vertical band searched for a handle opening
hem width that counts as a broad bag body

stages.name: Footwear cues
stages.computes: Re-frames the silhouette and mirrors it so the toe always points the same way. It then builds a smooth hull over the upper outline and measures the dark area inside it (open straps), columns with gaps between strap and sole, a sole that is filled at the front but empty at the back (backless), and overall height (a thin sole). These cues raise the sandal score and lower the sneaker and boot scores. A tongue peak in front of a scooped opening and a short height favour sneaker. A steep vertical front, a tall back and a cut-out under the heel favour boot.

key_numbers.meaning: fraction of the hull interior that is empty, from closed to open-strap
total item height below which the sole counts as thin, as on a flat sandal
height below which a shoe counts as low, as on a sneaker

key_numbers.value: 3 to 7 px rise; 9 to 16 px back height
key_numbers.meaning: front-edge jump and rear height that mark a boot shaft

stages.name: Garment-versus-bag guard
stages.computes: If the cue bonuses have pushed the best garment score above the best raw garment-style match, 62% of that excess is also given to bag. This stops rectangular bags being taken for clothing because of fabric cues. Further handle and broad-body bonuses are then added to bag.

key_numbers.meaning: share of the garment cue gain passed to bag

d.decision: The class with the highest final score wins. That score is the template-based prior for the class (a soft maximum over its styles' nearest-drawing scores) plus the sum of all hand-weighted cue adjustments.
d.adapts_per_image: Many steps depend on the particular image. Brightness is normalised by that image's own roughly 90th percentile pixel. The silhouette is cropped and rescaled to that image's bounding box. Template matching keeps only the 8 nearest drawings per style. Every garment cue is measured relative to a centre line found in that image, and some regions sit relative to the hem or item height found there. Shoes are mirrored when needed so the toe faces the same way. One placket cue keeps the best of several candidate positions, and the lapel test keeps the best of several V shapes. The bag score gets extra credit only when garment bonuses exceed the template baseline. There is no iteration until convergence.

d.summary: The item is turned into a soft silhouette and compared with about thirty thousand computer-drawn silhouettes of the ten kinds of clothing. For each class, the best-matching drawing in each of four batches is kept and the four best scores are averaged. These outline scores are then adjusted by hand-written evidence rules: how much of the item falls in fixed body regions (legs, skirt flare, shoulders, shoe shaft), dark gaps enclosed by the item (sandal straps, bag handles, the split between trouser legs), contrast-normalised detail detectors (button rows, plackets, lapels, ribbing, checks, necklines, hems, a continuous sole line), and bag-shape checks. The decision runs in two levels. The best outline score among tops (T-shirt, pullover, coat, shirt), and separately among footwear (sandal, sneaker, ankle boot), fixes how high that family scores. The detail evidence then picks the class inside the family.
d.references: Silhouette drawings made from code: 3072 per class, 30,720 in all. Each is a filled outline built from random shape parameters. Tops and dresses are drawn as torso plus sleeves, in styles such as tee, tank, long tee, sweater, tunic, jacket, overcoat, cardigan, button shirt, blouse, frock, sheath, gown, shift and skirt. Trousers get a waistband and two legs. Sneakers, ankle boots and sandals are drawn from the side (sandals as sole, heel and thin strap tubes). Bags are rounded boxes with an optional handle loop. Each drawing is cropped to its bounding box and scaled so its longest side fills 91 to 100% of the frame, with small random shifts, slight tilt and slight width stretch. Shoes and bags are also shifted downward. The drawing is then reduced to a 14x14 coverage grid and dimmed by a random brightness factor (0.65 to 0.99). For each drawing the stored values are its 14x14 coverage, its row and column profiles, coarse 3-band row and column profiles, and a 13x13 dilated version, plus a small style-specific penalty (for example long tees and tanks under T-shirt, tees under shirt, mirrored shoes). There are also about 200 fixed line and pattern probes on the 28x28 image (center-surround ridges, gratings, arcs), several dozen fixed region masks, and 72 horizontal sole-line probes. None of these is learned.

stages.name: Soft foreground mask
stages.computes: Each pixel's brightness goes through three overlapping linear ramps, weighted and summed into a 0 to 1 'item present' value. It is near 0 for black background and saturates to 1 for clearly lit pixels.

key_numbers.meaning: brightness levels where the three ramps start (grey level 0 to 1)
brightness levels where the three ramps saturate; at 0.29 and above a pixel counts as fully foreground
share of the foreground value each ramp contributes

stages.name: Coarse coverage grids
stages.computes: The mask is averaged over 2x2 pixel cells into a 14x14 coverage grid. A dilated 13x13 version takes the maximum over each 2x2 group of neighbouring cells.

key_numbers.meaning: coverage grid resolution (each cell is 2x2 image pixels)

stages.name: Silhouette matching against drawings
stages.computes: For every stored drawing, a score is computed that equals minus a weighted squared difference between the image and the drawing, minus the style penalty. The difference is taken on full coverage, row and column profiles, coarse 3-band profiles, and the dilated grid.

key_numbers.meaning: weight on the full 14x14 coverage difference
weights on column-profile and row-profile differences
weight on each coarse band profile (rows and columns grouped into bands of 4, 6 and 4 cells)
weight on the dilated-grid difference, which tolerates small misalignment

stages.name: Best match per class
stages.computes: Each class's 3072 drawings are split into 4 batches of 768. The best score in each batch is kept and the four bests are averaged into that class's outline score.

key_numbers.meaning: batches per class and drawings per batch

stages.name: Body-region occupancy and dark-gap detection
stages.computes: The share of each of 43 fixed regions that the item covers is measured: leg split, legs, waistband, bodice, widths at several heights, sleeve zones, shoe shaft, tongue, toe, heel, and so on. Separately, at 196 sample points (every other pixel), a point counts as an enclosed gap when it is empty, the item lies within 14 rows above and within 14 rows below it, and (strict version) its whole 3x3 neighbourhood is dark. Gap counts are averaged over four zones: lower middle (sandal holes), rear lower (back holes), upper middle (bag handles) and bottom centre (between trouser legs).

key_numbers.meaning: how far above and below a point the search for item pixels goes
penalty factor that makes the strict gap need a 3x3 neighbourhood darker than about 1/14 grey
examples of region edges: the leg-split strip is within 0.048 of the centre line and the legs lie 0.051 to 0.166 from centre, at heights 0.59 to 0.91 of the frame

stages.name: Proportion and gap rules
stages.computes: 27 hand-set rules combine region shares and gap counts linearly. Each result is turned into a 0 to 1 clipped ramp between a low and a high cutoff, and the ramp casts weighted votes for or against classes. Examples: leg coverage minus leg-split coverage votes trouser. Skirt or hem width exceeding waist width votes dress. Upper width exceeding skirt width votes T-shirt. Shaft coverage over tongue coverage votes ankle boot. Gaps in the lower middle vote sandal. Upper handle gaps vote bag. Low total coverage votes sandal.

key_numbers.meaning: ramp cutoffs for the legs-versus-split trouser rule (shares of region covered)
ramp cutoffs on the share of gap points in the sandal hole zone
ramp cutoffs on the share of gap points in the bag-handle zone

stages.name: Garment detail detectors
stages.computes: The image is standardised by its own mean and spread. It is then probed with fixed patterns: thin vertical ridges near the centre (placket, opening), off-centre verticals, V lapels, horizontal ribbing at the hem, stripes, check gratings, a chest emblem blob, a light/dark step at the centre front, shirt tail, periodic button rows on and off centre, neckline arcs and curved hems. Each family keeps its strongest absolute response. Rectified horizontal and vertical edge energy is also averaged over centre, upper, lower, side and narrow-centre zones.

key_numbers.meaning: centre-front positions tried for placket and front lines
button spacings tested along the centre front
heights tested for hem ribbing

stages.name: Detail rules for tops
stages.computes: 21 ramped rules combine detector strengths into small votes among T-shirt, pullover, coat and shirt. Plackets, openings, lapels and a front step favour coat and shirt. Ribbing, neck arcs and welt hems favour pullover. Button rows, checks and busy texture favour shirt. A graphic on the upper chest with a plain lower part favours T-shirt and pullover.

key_numbers.meaning: ramp cutoffs for the button-row rule (on-centre minus 0.74 x off-centre response), which casts the biggest shirt vote of 0.047
overall scale on all detail votes

stages.name: Footwear detail rules
stages.computes: Coverage is measured in toe, instep and ankle column bands and in their upper halves. The detector finds the strongest horizontal sole line that appears in both the front half and the back half (it takes the weaker half, so the line must run continuously), searched over 12 heights and 3 slopes. 6 ramped rules then vote among sandal, sneaker and ankle boot: a high ankle versus instep favours boot, a continuous sole without holes favours sneaker, and holes plus low coverage favour sandal.

key_numbers.meaning: range of sole-line heights searched (fraction of image height, step 0.036)
sole-line slopes tried (height change per image width)

stages.name: Bag verification
stages.computes: Two rules use these measurements: coverage of the left, right and middle column bands and of the whole image, the best-filled horizontal band out of 12 (6 heights x 2 widths), left-right coverage imbalance, and handle gaps. Only a net negative result is applied, and only to the bag score, so this stage can only veto bag.

key_numbers.meaning: centre heights of the pouch bands (fraction of image height, each band about 0.18 tall)
left and right side bands compared for imbalance

d.decision: The highest final score wins. Trouser, dress and bag score as outline match plus proportion and gap votes, with the bag score possibly vetoed. The four tops classes get the best coarse top score (outline plus proportion votes, top-specific votes left out). To that is added each class's fine score (outline plus all proportion votes plus detail votes) minus the best fine score among tops. The family level is therefore set by silhouette, and the choice inside the family by details. Footwear works the same way: each class gets the best outline score among sandal, sneaker and boot, plus its own outline, proportion and shoe-detail score minus the best such score within footwear.
d.adapts_per_image: Yes. Silhouette matching keeps the best of 768 drawings per batch, so it effectively searches over styles, sizes and small shifts. Each detail family keeps its strongest probe (a search over position, width and tilt). The sole line is searched over height and slope, with the weaker of the front and back halves kept. The best pouch band is chosen out of 12. Detail probes run on the image standardised by its own mean and spread. Within tops and within footwear, scores are measured against the best score in that family for this image.

d.summary: The item is first reduced to a soft silhouette. Its 14 x 14 outline, plus row-filled and column-filled versions of it, is compared with about ten thousand procedurally drawn clothing silhouettes, and each class keeps the score of its closest drawing. On top of that, a large set of hand-placed measurements adds evidence for and against classes: width and height, gaps between trouser legs, handle holes, shoe top-line profiles, strap voids, zip or placket lines, lapels, hems, cuffs and print texture. Classes are grouped into five families (tops, trousers, dresses, footwear, bags). Shape evidence mostly decides which family wins, and detail evidence picks the class inside it.
d.references: There are 10,240 synthetic silhouette drawings, 1,024 per class. Each is a polygon drawing generated with random parameters. Garment outlines (tee, tank, cap sleeve, long sleeve, knit, jacket, coat, long shirt, blouse, and dress variants) have parametric neck, shoulders, bust, waist, hip, hem and sleeves. Trousers have a waistband and two legs with random width and gap. Shoes are side views (sandal, high sandal, slide, sneaker, high top, boot, heel) with sole, heel and upper or straps. Bags (tote, bag, clutch, backpack, strap bag) have a rounded body and an arched handle. Each drawing is randomly stretched in width or height per class and slightly skewed, tilted and shifted. It is filled on a 56 x 56 canvas and averaged down to 14 x 14. Each stored drawing keeps three views: the filled shape (mixed with a smoothed copy), its filled extent along each row, and its filled extent along each column.

stages.name: Soft foreground mask
stages.computes: Each pixel's grey level becomes a 0 to 1 'is item' value. It rises steeply to about 0.79 at a faint level, then reaches full membership at a slightly brighter level.

key_numbers.meaning: grey level (0 to 1 scale) where a pixel counts as about 0.79 foreground
grey level at which a pixel counts as fully foreground

stages.name: Coarse silhouette and row/column fills
stages.computes: The mask is averaged in 2 x 2 blocks to a 14 x 14 grid. For every row, each cell is set to the smaller of the brightest value to its left and the brightest value to its right, which fills the span between the leftmost and rightmost ink. The same is done down every column. Subtracting the original silhouette from these fills gives maps of enclosed gaps, such as space between legs, under arms or inside a handle.

key_numbers.meaning: coarse grid, each cell 2 x 2 image pixels

stages.name: Template matching against drawn silhouettes
stages.computes: The coarse silhouette and its row and column fills are compared with every stored drawing using a weighted squared difference. The weights are about 0.53 for the shape and about 0.23 and 0.24 for the row and column fills. Each class keeps only its best-matching drawing's score.

key_numbers.meaning: drawings per class searched for the best match
relative weight of shape, row fill and column fill in the match

stages.name: Full-resolution derived maps
stages.computes: At 28 x 28 the method builds several maps. (1) A closed outline: the mask grown and then shrunk by a 5 x 5 neighbourhood, which fills small notches. (2) Left-facing and right-facing side edges of that outline and of the raw mask. (3) Which columns and rows contain any ink, giving the width and height fractions. (4) Gap points: background pixels with ink two pixels away on both sides, horizontally, vertically or diagonally. (5) A brightness map, the raw grey level plus a share of the grey level standardised by this image's mean and spread. From that map it also takes local contrast: rectified horizontal and vertical brightness changes, vertical ridge lines and centre-versus-surround fine detail.

key_numbers.meaning: neighbourhood size used to close the outline
mix of raw grey level and per-image standardised grey level in the brightness map
gap-test distance to ink on opposite sides of a background pixel

stages.name: Shoe top-line profile
stages.computes: The coarse grid is split into five column bands from front to back (toe, instep, laces, throat, heel). For each band it measures how far up the image the item reaches, as the share of top-row cutoffs (rows 3 to 9 of 14) above which there is ink.

key_numbers.meaning: band positions on the 14-column coarse grid
range of top-of-item heights tested, on the 14-row grid

stages.name: Trouser and dress shape cues
stages.computes: It tests for trousers: an item narrower than 59% of the frame, the two leg columns filled with a gap between them in the lower body (several heights tested), a solid seat over an empty crotch, and a vertical background gap down the centre. Dresses gain from slim width, a wide lower hem compared with the waist (flare), a filled centre near the hem and a brightness band across the waist (belt). Both lose points when there are background gaps beside the body at arm height.

key_numbers.meaning: width below which narrowness evidence for trousers starts
left leg, centre gap and right leg regions (fractions of the image)
hem band compared with waist band for dress flare

stages.name: Bag cues
stages.computes: It rewards a background hole in the upper centre with filled shoulders on either side (a handle), filled top corners, an item wider than it is tall, a lower body much wider than its top, and an open inner region. It penalises arm gaps, notched side edges in the lower half, a heavier rear than front, an even top, and a rising heel profile.

key_numbers.meaning: range over which width minus height (fractions of the frame) builds bag evidence
region checked for an enclosed handle hole

stages.name: Footwear cues
stages.computes: Sneakers gain from a raised tongue region with a low area behind it, a lace peak above the throat and heel, a solid filled mid-section and a low flat profile. Ankle boots gain from a filled ankle region at the rear top and a heel line that rises in steps. Sandals gain from holes inside the closed outline, gap points and perforation-like enclosed spaces in the middle band, empty space in the mid-section and toe, and an open rear.

key_numbers.meaning: tongue region compared with ankle region (sneaker against boot)
band where holes in the closed outline mark sandal straps
mid-section fullness band

stages.name: Upper-body garment detail cues
stages.computes: This stage separates T-shirt, pullover, coat and shirt. It looks for a vertical zip or placket line in brightness near the centre columns (12 to 15), diagonal lapel lines from the shoulders, a left-right brightness step from overlapping fronts and a brighter or darker front panel. It also measures contrast at the collar compared with the chest, small isolated chest detail (a logo), horizontal stripes, busy print texture in four chest and belly quadrants, hem lines, a curved shirttail, sleeve cuffs reaching the bottom corners (pullover), a T-shirt step from wide shoulders to a narrower body, short sleeves (shoulder filled, underarm empty) and an upright collar.

key_numbers.meaning: centre columns checked for a zip or placket line
bottom band where corner cuffs and the centre hem are compared
upper and lower body widths compared for the T-shirt taper

stages.name: Evidence shaping and vote totals
stages.computes: Each measurement is turned into a ramp that saturates between two hand-set limits. Some ramps are added together and ramped again to form combined cues (pant-like, long-armed, collar, print, sneaker vamp, big opening, open heel, dress belt). Weighted sums give two sets of class votes: detailed votes for each class, and coarse family-level votes in which all tops share one prior and all footwear share another. Fixed class offsets are added: +0.8 T-shirt, +1.6 pullover, -1.25 coat, -3.7 shirt, -1.0 sandal.

key_numbers.meaning: fixed handicap on the shirt class score
fixed bonus on the pullover class score

stages.name: Family-calibrated combination
stages.computes: Fine score = template score + detailed votes. Broad score = template score + family votes. Within each family (tops; trousers; dress; sandal, sneaker and boot; bag) the class order follows the fine score. The family's level is moved so its best member scores 0.2 x best fine + 0.8 x best broad.

key_numbers.meaning: share of the family-level (broad) evidence in setting each family's top score

d.decision: The final class is the highest of the ten calibrated scores. In practice the broad evidence (outline match plus family cues) mostly decides which family wins, and the fine evidence picks the member within that family.
d.adapts_per_image: The method searches each class's 1,024 stored drawings and keeps the closest one. The row and column fills and the closed outline depend on where this image's ink lies. Part of the brightness map is standardised by the image's own mean and spread. The method also takes the best class within each family and uses it to set the family's score level. Everything else is a fixed computation with no iteration.

d.summary: The item's silhouette is cleaned up and compared with about 13,000 synthetic silhouettes drawn procedurally from 12 sub-types of garment, bag and shoe. For each sub-type, the closeness of its 5 nearest drawings becomes a shape score. Many hand-built measurements of the outline and of the fabric texture inside it (legs separated by a gap, flared hem, centre-front placket or zip, hood or collar rise, how far the sleeve ends hang, all-over print, holes and straps in footwear, boot shaft height) are then added to or subtracted from those scores with hand-set weights. Upper-body garments are scored first as one family and then by style. Footwear is settled by a two-step rule: open or closed, then boot or sneaker.
d.references: 13,375 procedurally drawn binary silhouettes, made with a fixed random seed. Each is a parametric shape with randomised proportions, drawn at 56 x 56, rescaled to a random aspect ratio and scale, shifted slightly and box-averaged down to 28 x 28. The counts by sub-type are: tee 950, tank 425, knit sweater 1500, outerwear 1500, long-sleeve shirt 1300, short-sleeve blouse 800, dress 1700, trousers (two legs split below a crotch) 750, bag (rounded box, sometimes with a looped handle) 1300, sandal (thin sole with 1 to 3 arched straps, sometimes a heel and an ankle strap) 1400, sneaker (low profile with tongue and collar) 750, boot (tall shaft at the back with a heel cut) 1000. Torso garments are a body that narrows and widens through shoulder, chest, waist and hip, with a scooped neck hole and sleeves that taper to a cuff. Each drawing is kept as a 133-number shape summary: a 7 x 7 grid of block coverage, the 14-band row and column coverage profiles, and the top, bottom, left and right outline depths in 14 bands each.

stages.name: Brightness normalisation and silhouette extraction
stages.computes: The image is divided by its brightest pixel. A lightly blurred copy is mixed in, and a soft foreground map is made with a threshold that adapts to each image's peak brightness. Thin dark cracks are closed by a one-pixel grow-then-shrink, and a hard silhouette is taken from the result. The unclosed soft map is kept for finding holes.

key_numbers.meaning: Foreground threshold: 26% of the blurred peak brightness, capped at 0.12 grey level. The soft edge ramps from 0.27x to 1.5x this threshold.
Weight given to the crack-closed silhouette when it is merged back into the soft map
Soft-map level above which a pixel counts as part of the hard silhouette

stages.name: Shape matching against stored drawings
stages.computes: The same 133-number shape summary is built for the image: block coverage, row and column profiles, and outline depths from each side. It is compared with every stored drawing by squared distance. For each of the 12 sub-types, the 5 closest drawings are averaged into a closeness score.

key_numbers.meaning: Block size for the 7 x 7 coverage grid
Coverage level that marks the outline edge when outline depths are measured
Number of nearest drawings averaged per sub-type
Relative weights of outline depths and row/column profiles in the distance

stages.name: Global silhouette geometry
stages.computes: Finds the bounding box from rows and columns with at least 2 silhouette pixels, which gives width, height and aspect. It measures left-right asymmetry against the best mirror line near the centre, and silhouette widths in horizontal bands at fixed fractions of the item's height (bust, waist, hip, hem, top belt). From these come flare (hem wider than waist), straightness and body curve.

key_numbers.meaning: Aspect (width/height) range over which the item is judged 'wide', which pushes away from garments
Bust, waist, hip and hem bands as fractions of the item's height from its top
Aspect range over which the item is judged 'narrow' (tall, like trousers or a dress)

stages.name: Leg-gap detection
stages.computes: Looks for a dark vertical gap near the centre columns with fabric on both sides in the lower part of the image. It also traces the best connected dark path upward from hem to crotch, which may drift one column per row with a penalty. This decides whether there are two separate legs. A wide, flat waistband is a further trouser cue.

key_numbers.meaning: Central columns searched for the inseam gap
Lower image rows where the leg gap is sought
Penalty for the dark path stepping one column sideways per row

stages.name: Upper-garment detail cues
stages.computes: Measures several kinds of interior evidence. One is a persistent vertical line of contrast at centre front (placket or zip) compared with the nearby fabric. Others are a V-shaped lapel edge pattern near the top centre, and whether the shoulders rise above the neck (hood or standing collar) or dip below it (scooped neck). It compares where the sleeve ends and the torso hem end vertically (a knit band above the cuffs, or a shirt tail or cuff below), and checks for black gaps between torso and hanging sleeves. It also measures texture: all-over print, a chest graphic, checks in both directions versus stripes in one, and print on the side panels. Neckline contrast arcs at shallow versus deep curves separate crew necks from open collars.

key_numbers.meaning: Central band compared with the flank bands for the front-closure line
Fraction of the half-width beyond which the lowest pixel counts as the sleeve cuff
Upper and lower torso windows compared for chest graphic versus all-over print
Neckline arc depths treated as crew neck versus deep or open collar

stages.name: Footwear openness cues
stages.computes: Inside each column's top-to-bottom envelope it measures the empty background (porosity). Other measures are notches in the top outline, enclosed holes found in both directions, straps hanging over gaps, a thin instep, a low back near the heel, low fill and a very flat aspect. Together these say whether the shoe is open (strappy) or closed.

key_numbers.meaning: Fraction of the envelope that is empty, ramping to 'open shoe'
Grey levels that mark a pixel as material when holes and suspended straps are found
Aspect range where a very flat, wide item is taken as a sandal
Start of the heel region as a fraction of the item's width from the left

stages.name: Boot versus sneaker cues
stages.computes: Measures the column heights at the toe, tongue, ankle, heel and collar positions, all as fractions of the item's width. Taller at the heel than the toe means tilt. Further cues are a high, flat collar plateau at the back (boot shaft) versus a tongue that crests in front of the collar (sneaker), and a squarer aspect (boot).

key_numbers.meaning: Toe and heel regions as fractions of the item's width
Collar height as a fraction of item height, ramping to 'tall shaft'
Aspect range over which squarer shapes count toward boot
Columns whose top lies within this fraction of the top of the item count toward the flat 'crown'

stages.name: Score combination
stages.computes: Each class score starts from its matching sub-type closeness score (the best of tee and tank, the best of shirt and blouse, and so on). A shared penalty for asymmetric or wide shapes is applied to garments, and hand-weighted sums of the cues above are added. For the four upper-body classes, the family strength is the best of the short-form, long-form and blouse-form scores. Each style score is taken relative to the best style score and added to it. Footwear gets a single family score.

key_numbers.meaning: Weight of the front-opening/hood/lapel cue on the coat score, the largest single cue weight
Weight of the leg-gap evidence on the trouser score
Cutoff on the boot-style score separating ankle boot from sneaker

d.decision: The class with the highest combined score is chosen. Sandal, sneaker and ankle boot share one family score, but only one of the three is allowed per image. It is sandal if the open-construction evidence beats the closed-construction evidence. Otherwise it is ankle boot if the boot-style score exceeds 0.84, else sneaker. That footwear score then competes with the garment and bag scores.
d.adapts_per_image: The method adapts to each image in several ways. Brightness is normalised by the image's own peak, and the foreground threshold is set from it. The shape match keeps the 5 nearest drawings per sub-type, found by sorting distances. All silhouette bands and regions are placed relative to the image's own bounding box, and texture cues are divided by the image's own mean brightness. Symmetry uses the best of 3 mirror positions. The leg detector takes the best of several central columns and runs a best-path search. Collar, lapel and closure detectors take the best over several candidate shapes and positions. Upper-body style scores are re-centred on the best style for that image. Footwear goes through a hard two-step branch (open versus closed, then boot versus sneaker).

clusters.approach: Soft silhouette on a 14x14 grid matched against procedurally drawn class silhouettes (best match per class or per batch), plus hand-set ramped shape, gap and texture rules, decided in two levels: silhouette-dominated coarse scores set the level of the tops and footwear families, and detail evidence ranks classes within each family

Soft silhouette summarised as a coverage grid plus outline depth profiles from the four edges (B and C crop and rescale first), k-nearest-neighbour distance to procedurally drawn class or sub-type silhouettes giving per-class shape scores, then additive hand-weighted geometric and texture cues, with partial grouping of upper-body classes (and F's rule-based footwear split)

pairs.shared: Soft silhouette, coarse grid plus edge-based outline maps compared with procedurally drawn per-class silhouettes, hand-set shape rules (leg gap, neckline, straps, handle) and texture cues (zip, placket) added per class
pairs.differs: B crops and stretches to the bounding box, uses depth profiles and aspect ratio, 16-NN with mirroring; A uses edge-reachability maps and best match per group, and makes a two-level family decision where B only groups upper-body classes

pairs.shared: Soft silhouette, 14x14 grid with edge-based outline features matched against procedurally drawn silhouettes, many hand-built shape and texture cues added to class scores
pairs.differs: C crops and rescales, scores 43 styles by 8-NN and pools them through a soft maximum prior, and decides in one flat step with a bag guard; A uses best match per group and a two-level family decision

pairs.shared: Ramped soft mask, 14x14 coverage, about 15 to 30k drawn silhouettes split into 4 batches per class with per-batch bests combined, ramped shape and gap rules, fabric detail detectors, handle detection, and a two-level decision where the best coarse outline score fixes the tops and footwear family levels and details rank within them
pairs.differs: Feature details: A uses edge-reachability maps, D uses row and column profiles plus a dilated grid; D's bag stage can only veto

pairs.shared: Ramped soft mask, 14x14 grid with enclosure features (reachability versus row and column fills), best match against drawn per-class silhouettes, ramped shape, gap, handle and texture cues, family-calibrated decision where coarse evidence sets the family level and fine evidence ranks members
pairs.differs: E keeps a single best drawing per class and mixes broad and fine scores 0.8 and 0.2 across five families; A combines group bests with a 0.55/0.45 mix and calibrates only tops and footwear

pairs.shared: Soft silhouette matched against procedurally drawn silhouettes, then hand-weighted shape cues (leg gap, flare, straps, shaft) and texture cues (placket, print), with upper-body classes treated as a family
pairs.differs: F uses 5-NN per sub-type over a coverage plus depth descriptor and settles footwear by a rule chain (open, then boot or sneaker); A uses reachability maps, group bests and a symmetric two-level calibration

pairs.shared: Crop and rescale to the bounding box, coarse coverage grid plus four edge depth profiles, k-NN distance blending the mean of the closest drawings with the single closest, many additive shape and texture cues, highest score wins
pairs.differs: C scores 43 styles and pools them into classes through a soft maximum with a garment-versus-bag guard; B matches per class with mirroring, keeps aspect ratio as a feature and rebuilds upper-body scores from shared group scores

pairs.shared: Soft silhouette compared with tens of thousands of drawn per-class silhouettes, then hand-set geometric and texture cues adjusting class scores, with tops grouped
pairs.differs: B crops to the box and uses k-NN on depth profiles; D uses best per batch on coverage and profile features and a full two-level calibration for tops and footwear

pairs.shared: Silhouette template match against drawn per-class silhouettes, hand-set geometry and texture cues per class, some grouping of tops
pairs.differs: B crops and uses 16-NN on depth profiles with partial upper-body rebuilding; E uses best single match on grid plus fills and a family-calibrated two-level decision

pairs.shared: Coverage grid plus outline depth descriptor, k-NN averaged distance per class or sub-type, additive hand-weighted shape and texture cues, upper-body family score with relative style scores
pairs.differs: F matches 12 sub-types and settles footwear by a rule chain; B matches per class with mirroring and uses additive footwear cues

pairs.shared: Soft silhouette, 14x14 coverage matched against drawn silhouettes of many styles, hand-built shape, gap and texture cue adjustments
pairs.differs: C crops, uses 8-NN per style with a soft maximum class prior and a flat decision; D uses per-batch bests with style penalties and a two-level family decision

pairs.shared: Soft silhouette, 14x14 grid template matching against drawn style silhouettes, many ramped shape and texture cues
pairs.differs: C crops, uses k-NN per style with a soft maximum prior and a flat decision; E uses best single match per class with fill maps and family calibration

pairs.shared: Silhouette summarised by coverage plus edge depths, k-NN per style or sub-type pooled into class scores, additive hand-weighted shape and texture cues
pairs.differs: C pools by soft maximum with a bag guard and a flat decision; F takes the best sub-type, uses an upper-body family score and settles footwear by a rule chain

pairs.shared: Ramped soft mask, 14x14 coverage plus row and column style features, best matches against drawn per-class silhouettes, ramped region and gap rules, detail detectors, family-level decision set by coarse evidence with details ranking within each family
pairs.differs: D averages four batch bests and calibrates only tops and footwear; E keeps one best per class and blends broad and fine scores 0.8 and 0.2 across five families

pairs.shared: Silhouette template match with hand-set shape, gap and texture rules, tops and footwear handled as families
pairs.differs: F uses 5-NN per sub-type on depth descriptors and a rule chain for footwear; D uses batch bests and a symmetric coarse-then-fine calibration

pairs.shared: Silhouette template match with hand-set shape and texture cues, families for tops and footwear
pairs.differs: E uses a best single match and family calibration for all five families; F uses 5-NN per sub-type, relative style scores for tops and a footwear rule chain

steps.step: Soft foreground mask with thresholds normalised to the image's own brightness (peak, 90th percentile)
steps.note: All networks build a soft 0 to 1 mask, but from fixed absolute grey levels (N1 0.009/0.045/0.16, N2 three ramps, N3 0.045/0.145). None rescales by the image's peak or percentile.

steps.step: Crop to bounding box and rescale to fill a fixed frame (removes position and size)
steps.note: No network crops. All match in the raw image frame. Templates drawn with random scale, offset and stretch (N1 narrow 0.94 to 1.04, N2 91 to 100% fill with shifts, N3 random stretch) stand in for normalisation. P3 also matches in the fixed frame.

steps.step: Morphological crack closing of the silhouette (grow then shrink)
steps.note: N3 closes with a 5x5 neighbourhood, but only for its full-resolution derived maps, not for the matched silhouette. P3 uses a one-pixel close to build the hard silhouette.

steps.step: Coarse coverage grid descriptor
steps.note: All networks use 14x14 grids of 2x2 cells, the same as P2's grid (P1 12x12, P3 7x7). The networks build theirs in the raw frame, P2 in the cropped frame. N1 adds a mean/max mix and a noise floor. N2 adds a dilated 13x13 grid.

steps.step: Edge-to-outline depth profiles from the four sides
steps.note: N1 stores per-cell soft reachability from each edge instead of band-averaged first-hit depths, which encodes the same outline information. N3's row and column fills (min of the left and right running max) encode the outline spans from opposite sides. N2 has only coverage profiles, no depths.

steps.step: Row and column coverage profiles in the descriptor
steps.note: N2 uses row and column profiles plus coarse 3-band profiles. N3 uses filled extents, not sums.

steps.step: Aspect ratio as an explicit descriptor feature
steps.note: In the networks the aspect ratio is only implicit in the fixed-frame grid. N3 uses width and height fractions as cues, not in matching.

steps.step: Nearest-drawing matching with k-nearest averaging (sort, keep k, blend mean and min)
steps.note: The programs sort and keep the k nearest (16, 8, 5). The networks take minima over fixed partitions instead: N1 0.55 x best of 4 group bests + 0.45 x their mean, N2 the mean of 4 batch bests, N3 the single best (k=1). The goal is the same, but the robust k-NN statistic is replaced.

steps.step: Pooling sub-style scores into class scores (soft max or best of styles with mixing weights)
steps.note: The networks have no style table. Styles are mixed into each class's template pool, so the per-class minimum implicitly maxes over styles. N2 adds per-style penalties in place of mixing weights.

steps.step: Mirrored matching or orientation flip for footwear
steps.note: N2 includes mirrored shoe drawings, with a penalty, in its template pool. No network flips the input so the toe points one way. All shoe cues assume a fixed orientation.

steps.step: Garment width profile at shoulder, waist, hip and hem bands
steps.note: Bands are fixed fractions of the image (N1 waist 0.38 to 0.58 against P3's 0.38 to 0.57 of the item box). The programs place bands relative to the item's box or stretched frame.

steps.step: Trouser leg-gap test (empty centre slit with legs on both sides)
steps.note: N1 probes 27 slanted lines with flanking-leg spacings and keeps the best, the closest to P3's path search. N2 uses enclosed-gap counts and the legs-minus-split region. N3 uses fixed leg and gap regions at several heights. All use fixed image positions, not P2's found centre line or P3's per-image box.

steps.step: Waistband (full flat top band) cue
steps.note: N1 tests 27 top bands for full coverage. N2 has a waistband region. N3 only mentions a solid seat over the crotch.

steps.step: Skirt flare / dress cues (hem wider than waist, narrow item)
steps.note: These are ramped differences of fixed-region widths. N3 adds slimness below 0.59 of frame width.

steps.step: Sleeve length: cuff height versus hem, sleeve overhang
steps.note: N1 uses cuffs above the hem and the T-step span difference. N2 uses sleeve zones and upper width over skirt. N3 uses corner cuffs at the bottom band and a shoulder-filled, underarm-empty test. The programs locate the lowest pixel near the side per image.

steps.step: Air gaps between hanging sleeves and body
steps.note: N1 measures gaps beside the hem. N2 uses enclosed-gap points. N3 uses arm-height background gaps, mainly as a penalty on dress and trousers.

steps.step: Neckline rise versus scoop (collar or hood against scooped neck)
steps.note: N1 uses neck-above-shoulder top depth. N2 uses neckline arc probes. N3 uses an upright-collar cue and collar contrast. The programs search wedge or arc sizes relative to the found centre.

steps.step: Centre-front zip or placket line, compared against side panels
steps.note: P1 searches tilts and offsets. P2 measures along the image's own centre line. The networks use fixed centre strips (N1 |x|<0.066 against flanks, N3 columns 12 to 15) or a small fixed position set (N2 12.8 to 15.2 px), plus best-of templates.

steps.step: Button or bright-point row along the centre front
steps.note: N2 tests periodic button rows at 3 spacings.

steps.step: Lapel or V-wedge edges below the neck
steps.note: These are fixed V and lapel probes with the strongest kept, in place of V shapes placed relative to the found centre or neck.

steps.step: Chest logo against all-over print
steps.note: N2 uses a chest emblem blob and an upper-graphic, plain-lower rule. N3 uses isolated chest detail and four print quadrants. N1 has no chest-graphic cue.

steps.step: Directional texture: stripes in one direction against checks in both
steps.note: N1 takes the weaker of horizontal and vertical grating energy as plaid. N2 uses check gratings and edge energy by zone. N3 uses horizontal stripes and busy texture.

steps.step: Horizontal ribbed or waistband line near the hem
steps.note: These are fixed hem-rib probes (N2 rows 20 to 24.5). N3 uses hem lines.

steps.step: Curved shirt-tail hem
steps.note: N1 has rounded hems only in its templates.

steps.step: Interior brightness normalisation for texture cues
steps.note: The networks standardise by the image's mean and spread (N1 clips at -2/+2.8, N3 mixes with the raw grey level). The programs use the 80th percentile, the 90th percentile or the mean (P3, closest).

steps.step: Footwear openness: holes, strap voids, envelope porosity
steps.note: N1 uses enclosed vertical gap area in toe and arch zones. N2 uses gap points in the lower-middle zone. N3 uses holes in the closed outline and gap points. The programs use per-column envelopes or a hull on the oriented silhouette.

steps.step: Boot shaft: rear or shaft height above the toe
steps.note: N1 uses rear minus 0.8 x front height. N2 uses shaft over tongue coverage. N3 uses a filled ankle region and a stepped heel line. These are fixed regions with no flip.

steps.step: Sneaker tongue rise and drop
steps.note: N1 uses top-profile depth at instep and throat. N2 uses tongue region coverage. N3 uses the tongue against a low area behind it and a lace peak.

steps.step: Footwear flatness, low height and low fill
steps.note: N2 has a low-total-coverage sandal vote. N3 has a low flat profile and an empty mid-section. N1 is unclear (low heel counter, ankle notch).

steps.step: Hard two-step footwear branch (open or closed, then boot if the score exceeds 0.84)
steps.note: The networks rank footwear classes by summed scores within a re-anchored group. There is no hard branch.

steps.step: Bag handle hole above a solid body
steps.note: N1 uses a fixed bank of 160 handle templates and keeps the best. N2 uses the upper-middle enclosed-gap zone. N3 uses a fixed handle-hole region. P2 places its band relative to the item's height.

steps.step: Broad, symmetric or rectangular bag body
steps.note: N2 measures band coverage and left-right imbalance, but can only veto bag. N3 uses wider-than-tall, filled corners and a wide lower body.

steps.step: Garment-versus-bag guard (62% of excess garment cue gain passed to bag)
steps.note: N2's bag veto is a different mechanism.

steps.step: Left-right asymmetry penalty on garments (best of 3 mirror lines)
steps.note: N2's imbalance applies only to bag. N3's rear-heavy test is a bag penalty.

steps.step: Upper-body family score, then style scores relative to the best style
steps.note: In the networks, each group's best is re-anchored to a coarse silhouette-led score and fine evidence ranks within the group. The structure is similar, but the family level comes from template plus construction votes, not from best-of routes.

steps.step: Shirt score as best of alternative routes (tee-like, long-sleeve, blouse)
steps.note: In the networks, shirt is a single weighted sum.

steps.step: Final additive scoring and argmax
steps.note: The class with the highest score wins.

network_only.step: Two-level decision: the tops and footwear groups are shifted so their best equals a coarse score (silhouette only for footwear, silhouette + 0.38 x construction for tops). Fabric and handle evidence only ranks within a group. P3 has a footwear family score, but not this re-anchoring.
Fixed bank of 160 bag-handle templates (crown, legs, hole penalty), matched by best response above an offset of -0.53
Noise floor subtracted from the coarse grid and a 0.84 mean / 0.16 max cell mix
Dilated 13x13 grid term in the template distance, giving misalignment tolerance
Per-drawing style penalties added to the template score
Continuous sole-line detector searched over 12 heights and 3 slopes, keeping the weaker of the front and back halves
Bag verification that can only veto bag (only the negative part is applied)
Two-level family re-anchoring for both tops and footwear (best coarse score plus fine minus best fine)
Fixed class offsets (+0.8 T-shirt, +1.6 pullover, -1.25 coat, -3.7 shirt, -1.0 sandal)
Family calibration over five families: best member set to 0.2 x best fine + 0.8 x best broad
Brightness band across the waist as a dress belt cue
Gap points: background pixels with ink 2 px away on opposite sides in 4 directions

numbers.meaning: Coarse coverage grid resolution
numbers.program_values: P2 14x14 (2x2 blocks of the cropped, rescaled 28 frame)
numbers.network_values: N1, N2, N3 14x14 (2x2 cells of the raw 28x28 image)

numbers.meaning: Waist band height
numbers.program_values: P3 0.38 to 0.57 of the item's bounding-box height
numbers.network_values: N1 y 0.38 to 0.58 of image height

numbers.meaning: Hem band height
numbers.network_values: N1 y 0.81 to 0.95 of image height; N3 hem band y 0.78 to 0.91

numbers.meaning: Near-black level below which a pixel is background
numbers.network_values: N1 1/48 ≈ 0.021 (raw grey level, leg-gap black map)

numbers.meaning: Narrowness threshold for trouser or dress items
numbers.network_values: N3 0.59 of frame width

numbers.meaning: Leg-gap search region (lower centre)
numbers.program_values: P1 rows 15 to 23 of 24, columns 9 to 15; P3 columns 11 to 16, rows 10 to 26 of 28

numbers.meaning: Centre-front placket strip
numbers.program_values: P3 columns 9 to 14 of 28; P2 within 2.8 px of the found centre line
numbers.network_values: N3 columns 12 to 15 of 28; N2 x 12.8 to 15.2 px; N1 |x|<0.066

cover.verdict: The networks share the programs' overall plan: a soft silhouette, then nearest-template matching against procedurally drawn parametric outlines, then hand-weighted additive cues for legs, flare, sleeves, neckline, placket, lapels, texture, straps, shaft, tongue and handle, then an argmax. But almost every step is a fixed-frame approximation, not the same computation. Where the programs adapt per image, the networks use fixed absolute thresholds and fixed image regions with best-of over fixed probe banks: there is no peak or percentile brightness normalisation, no bounding-box crop and rescale, no found centre line, no toe-direction flip, and the sorted k-nearest averaging becomes minima over fixed batches. The networks leave out the explicit aspect feature, the edge-depth descriptor (in N2), footwear orientation, P2's garment-to-bag guard, P3's asymmetry penalty and hard two-step footwear branch, and the best-of-routes shirt score. They add a two-level family re-anchoring (plus fixed class offsets in N3) that the programs have only in partial form.

d.summary: The image is turned into maps of local evidence: oriented edges in 8 signed directions, small bright and dark spots, and fine detail that is lighter or darker than its surroundings. These maps are compared with the same maps computed from 15,360 synthetic renderings of a 3D tube-model hand making each letter (640 varied poses per letter). Each letter's score adds up its best-matching rendering in each of 8 batches of 80, where the upper and lower halves of the hand can each shift by up to about 2 pixels, independently, to line up.
d.references: Yes, rendered templates. For each of the 24 letters, 640 synthetic greyscale hand images (15,360 in total) are rendered at 40 x 40 from a hand-built 3D model. Each finger, the thumb, the palm and the forearm is a chain of tapered tubes with depth, hidden-surface removal, directional shading with a random light direction, a soft cast shadow and a slight blur. The model has three hand families: front-facing hands (A, B, D, E, F, I, K, L, M, N, R, S, U, V, W, X, Y), with per-letter finger extension, finger tilt, curl, thumb tip position and yaw; a curved hand for C and O, which differ in whether the curve closes; and sideways or downward hands for G, H, P, Q and T. Each rendering randomises finger lengths and widths, curl depth, yaw, in-plane roll, horizontal and vertical scale, shear (side hands only), hand size (21 to 32 grid units across its extent), position (about +/-2.9 horizontal, -2.1 to +2.8 vertical), background brightness (0.47 to 0.86), skin tone (0.37 to 0.61), shading strength, and a background brightness offset cycling through 5 values (-0.24, -0.09, 0, +0.09, +0.17). The same evidence maps are computed from each rendering, which is then cropped to the central 28 x 28 region at 14 x 14 cell resolution, reweighted and normalised to unit energy, and split into an upper-hand and a lower-hand version.

stages.name: Global exposure normalisation
stages.computes: Subtracts the image's mean brightness and divides by its brightness spread, so overall brightness and contrast no longer matter.

stages.name: Mirror the border
stages.computes: Extends the 28 x 28 photo by mirroring 5 pixels outward on every side, so that local measurements near the edge have surroundings to work with.

key_numbers.meaning: pixels of mirrored margin added on each side (28 to 38)

stages.name: Local evidence maps
stages.computes: At each pixel, measures 12 kinds of local evidence: edge strength in 4 orientations (0, 45, 90 and 135 degrees), each split by which side is brighter, giving 8 signed directions; small bright spots and small dark spots, measured as a small centre against a wider surround; and fine detail, measured as how much the pixel is lighter, or darker, than a 9 x 9 smoothed neighbourhood. Only positive responses are kept.

key_numbers.meaning: blur width of the edge detectors, in pixels (5 x 5 support)
centre and surround widths of the spot detector, in pixels
size of the smoothing window that sets the reference level for fine detail

stages.name: Soft saturation
stages.computes: Responses above a ceiling are compressed: only 18% of the amount above the ceiling is kept, so a few very strong edges cannot dominate.

key_numbers.meaning: ceiling on response strength, in units of normalised image contrast
share of the excess above the ceiling that is removed

stages.name: Local tolerance spread
stages.computes: Each evidence value is combined with the strongest value of the same kind within its 3 x 3 neighbourhood, which tolerates features being slightly out of place.

key_numbers.meaning: neighbourhood, in pixels, over which the strongest response is taken

stages.name: Coarse cells
stages.computes: Averages the evidence over 2 x 2 pixel blocks, giving a 14 x 14 grid of cells for each of the 12 evidence kinds, then mirrors a 1-cell margin around that grid (16 x 16).

key_numbers.meaning: pixels per cell
cells of mirrored margin, which allows shifts of +/-1 cell (about +/-2 pixels)

stages.name: Template comparison at shifted positions
stages.computes: Correlates the cell grid with every stored rendering's evidence pattern, at 3 x 3 shifts of one cell. The upper-hand and lower-hand versions of each rendering are compared separately, and each keeps its own best shift, so the top and bottom of the hand can line up independently.

key_numbers.meaning: stored renderings (24 letters x 640 poses), each with an upper and a lower version

key_numbers.value: rows 0 to 4 at 0.85, falling to 0.15 by row 9
key_numbers.meaning: upper-hand weighting over the 14 cell rows (top to bottom); the lower version uses the complement
range of the shift search, about +/-2 pixels in each direction

stages.name: How templates are weighted (built in advance)
stages.computes: Before storage, each rendering's pattern is reshaped to stress the right cues. Edge evidence has 72% of its average over the directions removed, which stresses direction-specific edges; spot evidence has 31% of its average removed; fine detail is boosted by 10%. Each evidence kind's average over the image is mostly removed (95%). The top of the hand is emphasised over the bottom (a ramp from 1.15 to 0.84, except for P and Q), the bottom row is down-weighted further, and the pattern is scaled to unit strength. Near the hand outline, each edge is partly blended with the edge of opposite brightness, by 10% to 30%, so the match tolerates the hand being lighter or darker than the background.

key_numbers.meaning: share of the direction-averaged edge level removed from each edge direction
top-to-bottom emphasis ramp over the 14 cell rows (flat for P and Q)
share of opposite-brightness edge blended in, highest at the hand outline

stages.name: Combine the halves and pick the best pose
stages.computes: For each rendering, the upper-hand and lower-hand match scores are averaged. Within each of 8 batches of 80 renderings per letter, the letter keeps its single best-matching rendering.

key_numbers.meaning: batches of poses per letter; one best pose is kept from each batch

stages.name: Pool across batches
stages.computes: Adds the 8 per-batch best scores to give each letter's final score.

d.decision: The letter with the highest total wins. A letter's total is the sum, over 8 batches of its renderings, of the best match in each batch, where a rendering's match is the average of its upper-half and lower-half agreement, each taken at its own best shift.
d.adapts_per_image: Yes. Brightness and contrast are normalised using the image's own mean and spread. For each rendering, the upper and lower halves each search 3 x 3 positions (+/-2 pixels) and keep the best alignment, independently of each other. For each letter, the best-matching pose is chosen within each of 8 batches of 80. The 3 x 3 strongest-neighbour step also lets each feature's evidence move slightly with the image. Everything else is a fixed computation.

d.summary: The method compares each photo against a large bank of computer-rendered synthetic hands, nothing else. First it estimates where the hand is by marking pixels that are hard to reach from the top, left and right borders without crossing strong edges, plus pixels that differ from a background guessed along each row. It then crops a square around the hand at six slightly different framings and describes each crop by its coarse silhouette, local edge directions, fine creases, thin finger-like ridges and an outline signature. Each class is scored by how closely the crops match that class's rendered hands, using the best few matches.
d.references: About 2,880 rendered hand images per letter (60 batches of 48), so roughly 69,000 in total over the 24 letters. Each one is stored as its description (silhouette, edge directions, creases, ridges), not as pixels. The hands are built in 3D from tubes for the finger segments, thumb and forearm and from ellipsoids for the palm, knuckles and thumb base, then rendered at 36 x 36 and shrunk to 28 x 28. Two generators are used. About one third come from an articulated skeleton: four fingers plus a thumb, with joint bend and spread angles set per letter (fingers straight for B, index straight for D/G/L, index and middle spread for V, thumb spread out for L/Y, and so on). About two thirds come from hand-laid stylised 2D poses per letter (for example a sideways pointing index for G/H, downward fingers for P/Q, curled finger arcs for C/O). Each render is randomised: hand thickness, finger length and spread, viewing rotation (yaw, pitch and roll, with letter-specific ranges such as sideways for G/H/T and downward for P/Q), lighting direction, Lambertian shading, contact shadows and cast shadows, skin brightness 0.42 to 0.62 plus shading, a flat background of 0.44 to 0.88, a forearm leaving the frame, and the framing of the square crop. For three quarters of the batches the render is recropped with the same hand finder used on test photos, with random jitter in size (0.89 to 1.1x), sideways position (up to 3.9% of the side) and headroom (1.2 to 8.6%). The hand-likelihood map stored for each reference mixes the true rendered silhouette (0.53) with the photo-style estimate (0.47).

stages.name: Edge strength map
stages.computes: Lightly blurs the image and measures how sharply brightness changes at each pixel. Each image is normalised by its own strongest edge, and the result is capped so that no single edge dominates.

key_numbers.meaning: Edge strength counted as 'strong': 36% of the image's maximum edge strength
Lowest allowed strong-edge level, in brightness units per 2 pixels, so near-flat images are not amplified
Cap on normalised edge strength (times the strong level)

stages.name: Border reachability (hand likelihood)
stages.computes: For each pixel, works out how much edge must be crossed to reach the top, left or right border. It does this two ways: by straight horizontal and downward scans, and by a cheapest curved path (a soft flood fill from those borders, 18 sweeps). The bottom border is not a source because the wrist enters there. Pixels walled off by edges count as hand, and the two estimates are mixed 0.26 for the straight scans and 0.74 for the curved path.

key_numbers.meaning: Edge evidence accumulated from the side borders / top border that counts as fully inside
Path cost at which a pixel is treated as fully enclosed (hand)
Path cost along the top row is halved, so the top border spreads background easily
Number of sweep rounds in the flood fill, which limits how winding a path can be

stages.name: Row-wise background contrast
stages.computes: Guesses the background of each row by blending in a straight line between the median of its 3 leftmost pixels and the median of its 3 rightmost pixels. Pixels far from that guess, or on edges, count as hand. This cue gets up to 47% of the weight when the left and right ends of the row agree in brightness, and gives way to the reachability estimate when they do not.

key_numbers.meaning: Width in pixels of the border strips used to sample background
Largest share of the final hand map given to the background-difference cue
Brightness difference from the background guess that counts as clearly different
Left/right brightness mismatch scale that lowers trust in the row background guess

stages.name: Hand bounding box
stages.computes: Thresholds the hand map, gives less weight to columns near the left and right edges and to blobs far from the hand's horizontal centre, and lightly blurs it. It then finds the top and bottom from cumulative row mass. The left and right sides come from column mass weighted toward the upper part of the hand, so the forearm counts less.

key_numbers.meaning: Hand-map level below which a pixel is ignored
Half-width of the central band around column 13.5. Outside it, mass drops to as little as 25%
Half-width around the hand's centre of mass kept at full weight. Mass further out drops to 18%
Cumulative mass fractions that set top/bottom and left/right, with 1 px padding. Height is at least 9 px

stages.name: Six candidate crops
stages.computes: Builds a square crop whose top sits slightly above the hand top, with side = max(height, 1.08 x width, 15 px), and resamples it to 28 x 28. The six versions are: tight; the whole uncropped frame; shifted left and right by 5.5% of the side with 0.85 zoom; zoomed in to 0.77; and zoomed out to 1.13 with more headroom.

key_numbers.meaning: Smallest crop side in original pixels
Width margin factor when sizing the square
Headroom above the hand top as a fraction of the side (tight crop)
Zoom factors of the alternative crops relative to the hand-fitted square

stages.name: Appearance description per crop
stages.computes: Describes the crop in four parts, each scaled to unit length. (1) A 10 x 10 coarse hand silhouette from the hand map. (2) The strength of edges in 4 orientations (0, 45, 90, 135 degrees, sharply tuned and blind to polarity) on a 12 x 12 grid, with lower rows down-weighted and orientations balanced within each cell. (3) Fine creases (fine blur minus coarse blur, mostly inside the hand) on a 13 x 13 grid. (4) Thin bright or dark lines in 4 orientations, found by comparing a pixel with its neighbours 2 px across versus 2 px along the line, on a 9 x 9 grid. The parts are weighted 0.61, 0.76, 0.32 and 0.355.

key_numbers.meaning: Grid cells per side for silhouette, edge directions, creases and thin lines
Weight of the bottom edge-grid row (wrist zone), rising to 1 in the middle rows. The top row is 0.82
Relative weight of silhouette, edges, creases and thin lines in the match
Offset used to test for a thin line against its sides

stages.name: Outline signature
stages.computes: From the 10 x 10 silhouette, measures each row's width and centre offset and each column's height and offset. It keeps the strength of the 1st to 8th Fourier harmonics of each of these four profiles, which gives a shape signature that ignores shifts.

key_numbers.meaning: Silhouette level (after rescaling to 0 to 1) that counts as filled
Mass fractions defining each row's or column's extent
Number of harmonics kept per profile

stages.name: Matching against rendered hands
stages.computes: For each crop and each letter, computes the similarity to every reference of that letter as the description match plus 0.21 x the outline-signature match. It keeps the 6 best references and scores the crop as 0.6 x best + 0.4 x mean of those 6. A letter's score is its best score over the six crops.

key_numbers.meaning: Weight of the outline signature relative to the appearance description
Number of closest rendered references kept per letter
Mix of best match and mean of the top 6

d.decision: The letter with the highest score wins. A letter's score is its best score over the six crops, and each crop's score is 0.6 x its best reference match plus 0.4 x the mean of its 6 best matches among that letter's roughly 2,880 rendered hands.
d.adapts_per_image: The method adapts to each image in several ways. Edge strength is normalised by the image's own strongest edge. The background guess is made row by row from that image's border pixels, and it gets less weight when the left and right borders disagree. The flood fill finds paths specific to the image. The crop box comes from that image's hand map (centroid, cumulative-mass extents, focus around its centre of mass). Edge, crease and thin-line strengths are normalised by their mean over the image.
